paragraphs.text: Farming has always been a bet against the weather, and for most of history the only insurance was a full barn. Formal crop insurance is barely a century old, and for its first decades it was mostly sold by governments, because private insurers found the business unattractive for a reason that is easy to state: when a drought comes, it does not ruin one farm, it ruins every farm in the district at the same time. An insurer needs its losses to be independent of one another, and weather losses are the opposite of independent.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The traditional answer is indemnity insurance, in which a farmer insures a yield and is paid the difference if the harvest falls short. It is accurate and it is expensive to run. Someone has to visit the field, measure what grew and judge whether the loss was caused by hail or by neglect, and in a bad year that inspection has to happen on thousands of farms within a few weeks. The administrative cost can exceed a quarter of the premium, and on small farms it exceeds the payout often enough that the product is not offered at all.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The alternative is to insure a number rather than a field. Index insurance pays out when a measurement crosses a threshold — rainfall at a nearby station below a stated amount during a stated window, or a satellite measure of vegetation below its usual value — regardless of what happened on any particular farm. Nobody inspects anything, the payment can arrive within days, and the cost of running the scheme falls to a fraction of the indemnity model. The design is elegant and it introduces a problem that has kept the field busy ever since.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: That problem is called basis risk, and it is the gap between the index and the farmer. A farm twenty kilometres from the rain gauge may be dry when the gauge is wet; a crop may fail from disease in a year of perfect rainfall; a payout may arrive in a village where the harvest was fine. Farmers who receive nothing after a real loss do not buy the product a second time, and the trust that is lost in one bad season takes years to rebuild, which is why uptake in many pilot schemes collapses in year two.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Reducing basis risk is mostly a matter of better measurement. Denser networks of weather stations help but are expensive to maintain; satellite measures cover everything and are coarse; the most promising combinations use both, with the index calibrated against historical yields in each district rather than against rainfall alone. Where such calibration has been done carefully, the correlation between payouts and actual losses rises sharply, and so does the share of farmers who renew.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Demand is a separate puzzle. Even where a product is well designed and modestly priced, take-up without subsidy is usually low, and the reasons are the ones behavioural economists would predict: the premium is paid now and the benefit is uncertain and later, the product is hard to understand, and a farmer who has never seen a neighbour paid has no reason to believe the payment will come. Schemes that pay one visible claim early in their life grow faster than schemes with better mathematics and no story.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Governments therefore subsidise, and the subsidies have consequences that are not always intended. Cheap insurance makes risky planting rational, so farmers move onto marginal land and grow thirsty crops where the water does not reliably arrive; the insurance then pays for the failure, and the public pays for the insurance. Several long-running programmes have been criticised on exactly this ground, and the fix that is usually proposed — pricing that reflects the actual risk of the field — is politically difficult everywhere it has been tried.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: None of this means the idea has failed. Index products now cover tens of millions of small farms, most of them in countries where no insurer would have written a policy at all twenty years ago, and the evidence that insured farmers invest more — in fertiliser, in better seed, in a second season — is reasonably strong. The honest description is of a useful instrument with a known defect, sold in a market that needs public money to exist, which is an ordinary condition for insurance rather than a scandal.
paragraphs.label: H
